title: The Cosmos

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

summary: John C. Williams, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, delivered a speech on April 16, 2026, presenting an economic outlook characterized by heightened uncertainty due to the Middle East conflict. He stated the March FOMC meeting maintained the federal funds target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, with current inflation at 2.8 percent (PCE, February) and the unemployment rate at 4.3 percent. Williams expects real GDP growth of 2 to 2-1/2 percent for the year.
key_points: March FOMC meeting maintained federal funds target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent
Unemployment rate held at 4.3 percent since July 2025; labor market showing mixed signals with hard data stable but soft data suggesting gradual softening
Overall PCE inflation at 2.8 percent as of February; tariffs contributed 0.5 to 0.75 percentage points to inflation
Middle East conflict driving energy price increases with pass-through effects to airfares, groceries, fertilizer, and other consumer products
No significant second-round tariff effects detected; underlying inflation excluding imported goods moving in the right direction
Medium and longer-term inflation expectations remain well-anchored at levels consistent with the FOMC's 2 percent longer-run goal
Expects real GDP growth of 2 to 2-1/2 percent for the year
why_it_matters: The statement 'As a voting FOMC member, Williams provides insight into the Fed's current policy stance' should be verified - the source does not explicitly state Williams' voting status for 2026. Consider removing or qualifying this claim.
macro_context: The speech outlines a complex macro backdrop: energy-driven inflation headwinds from the Middle East conflict offset by tariff-driven disinflationary effects, with labor markets showing no clear direction. Williams emphasizes the 'unusual dynamics' of simultaneous upward and downward inflation pressures. The forecast for 2-2.5% GDP growth suggests the economy remains resilient. Inflation expectations being well-anchored is a key signal that the Fed believes transient factors won't become entrenched.
